lines.speaker: mark
lines.text: Miss Thorne! Look at the flower on the left. The one that has not opened.

lines.speaker: rosalind
lines.text: It is the unrecorded one. The flower from the edge of the map! Dear God, Mark, it is opening.

lines.speaker: zephyrine
lines.text: It is blooming, Rosalind. Tonight, in the Hall, just as the founder said it would.

lines.speaker: cornelia
lines.text: Everyone, stand very still. Mr Pluck, do not breathe on it.

lines.speaker: barnaby
lines.text: I wasn't going to breathe on it, Miss Wren. I wasn't going to breathe at all.

lines.speaker: rosalind
lines.text: There is a seed in its heart, and on the seed a tiny writing. It says: Deep Vaults. Open when the garden is lit.

lines.speaker: hugo
lines.text: Cold down here, and not a draught in sight. Odd. A cellar this deep ought to howl.

lines.speaker: barnaby
lines.text: Hugo, why is the Coal Scuttle full? Nobody's lit a furnace in twenty years.

lines.speaker: hugo
lines.text: Fresh coal. Not a speck of damp on it. Somebody's been stacking this since the spring.

lines.speaker: cornelia
lines.text: Then the Vaults have a housekeeper, Mr Pluck, and a very fond opinion of tidy edges.

lines.speaker: anjali
lines.text: Whoever it is, I hope they like soup. I am about to move in.

lines.speaker: anjali
lines.text: Wheat, barley, oats, all of it sound! Cornelia, I could weep. Not a weevil anywhere.

lines.speaker: aldous
lines.text: I counted four mice, Anjali, and each one carried an ear of corn as though it were on an errand.

lines.speaker: anjali
lines.text: Then they are paid staff. I shall not interfere with their wages.

lines.speaker: mark
lines.text: The sacks are stacked in a pattern, um. Every third one faces the wall. I think it's a way of marking the weeks.

lines.speaker: cornelia
lines.text: Marking the weeks for whom, Mr Bloom?

lines.speaker: sam
lines.text: Hinges, Cornelia. I know hinges the way a sommelier knows corks, and this one was oiled yesterday.

lines.speaker: hugo
lines.text: Nice work, too. Thin film, no drips. I'd hire him.

lines.speaker: sam
lines.text: Do not encourage me, Hugo. I am already halfway to admiring a burglar I have not met.

lines.speaker: prudence
lines.text: The oilcan sits on the shelf beside it, with a label in a very small hand: For the Wednesday round.

lines.speaker: cornelia
lines.text: A round, Miss Quill. A route, with a schedule. We are not the first to walk these stairs this month.

lines.speaker: barnaby
lines.text: Miss Wren, there's a ham missing from the end of the rack, and the cut's as clean as a ruler!

lines.speaker: anjali
lines.text: Barnaby is right. That slice was made with a blade I would be proud to own.

lines.speaker: zephyrine
lines.text: The crumbs lead off towards the passage on the left. Small crumbs. Very patient crumbs.

lines.speaker: rosalind
lines.text: A thief with manners, my dears. I find I am rather smitten.

lines.speaker: cornelia
lines.text: Nobody is to follow the crumbs until we have had lunch. That is an order.

lines.speaker: prudence
lines.text: Forty amphorae, every stopper sealed with a different port's wax. And a thirty-ninth that rattles.

lines.speaker: zephyrine
lines.text: The thirty-ninth is from Karsa, on the Southern Sea. Nobody trades with Karsa. It does not appear on any chart but mine.

lines.speaker: sam
lines.text: Then how did it get into a locked vault, Zephyrine?

lines.speaker: zephyrine
lines.text: I have been asking myself that since I first lifted it.

lines.speaker: aldous
lines.text: If it rattles, it is a gift of some kind. Open it, someone. I am at an age where I enjoy a rattle.

lines.speaker: cornelia
lines.text: At dinner, Professor, with forks, and a witness from every wing.

lines.speaker: aldous
lines.text: Garlic. A great deal of garlic. One does wonder whom the Society was keeping out.

lines.speaker: mark
lines.text: It's, um, just for cooking, Professor. I think. Though somebody hung it over the stair as well.

lines.speaker: barnaby
lines.text: Over the stair going down, Mark. Not over the one going up.

lines.speaker: anjali
lines.text: That means it is not guarding the Vaults from the world. It is guarding the world from the Vaults.

lines.speaker: cornelia
lines.text: Miss Bose, you have said an extremely unhelpful thing.

lines.speaker: cornelia
lines.text: Mr Vane, why are your boots dusty and your hands empty?

lines.speaker: sam
lines.text: I was looking at the scale, Cornelia. The little brass weights are all here, except the thousandth-of-a-grain one.

lines.speaker: prudence
lines.text: That weight is the whole accuracy of the instrument. Without it, it merely guesses.

lines.speaker: hugo
lines.text: There's a muddy print on the counter, size ten, with a gold-tipped heel. Does anyone wear gold on their heels?

lines.speaker: sam
lines.text: Only one man I know. Lucian Merrick has been in our Vaults.

lines.speaker: zephyrine
lines.text: The Guard's Lamp is lit, and it was not lit when we came down. Nobody has touched it.

lines.speaker: hugo
lines.text: I'll swear it on my spanners. The wick's not even wet.

lines.speaker: barnaby
lines.text: I left a biscuit by it, Miss Blackwood, just in case. And it's gone!

lines.speaker: aldous
lines.text: Biscuits do not vanish, Barnaby. They are eaten, or they are carried off, and there is a difference.

lines.speaker: rosalind
lines.text: In a house like this, my dears, I am inclined to think they are accepted.

lines.speaker: rosalind
lines.text: A Guard's Desk, a logbook, a pen with a split nib. How very touching, that someone kept watch down here.

lines.speaker: prudence
lines.text: The last entry in his hand: All quiet. The cat has the key. A drawing follows, of a cat wearing a very small hat.

lines.speaker: barnaby
lines.text: I knew it was the cat! I said so, Miss Quill, I said it on Tuesday!

lines.speaker: zephyrine
lines.text: A cat holds the keys to the Deep Vaults and has done for twenty years. I do not find that more remarkable than half the people I know.

lines.speaker: sam
lines.text: Nor I. Most of them cannot even be trusted with the umbrella.

lines.speaker: hugo
lines.text: That clock has been running since before the Hall had gas, and it says a quarter to twelve.

lines.speaker: aldous
lines.text: It said a quarter to twelve in the Study too, Hugo. And in the dictionary, I am told.

lines.speaker: hugo
lines.text: Different clocks, different makers, and they all agree. Clocks don't agree. They fight.

lines.speaker: prudence
lines.text: Unless someone has set them all to the same hour on purpose, and then walked away.

lines.speaker: cornelia
lines.text: Then someone has left the Hall waiting for a quarter to twelve. I should like to be there when it arrives.

lines.speaker: anjali
lines.text: It's not a tomb, Barnaby. Lift the lid. Gently. Tureens first, then the soup spoons.

lines.speaker: barnaby
lines.text: Forty soup plates, and a ladle shaped like a swan! Miss Bose, you were right!

lines.speaker: sam
lines.text: Who hides a dinner service in a sarcophagus? Rosalind, it is the cleverest idea in the Hall.

lines.speaker: rosalind
lines.text: It is the cleverest in three centuries, Sam, and it was mine. I did it after the dinner party that ended in a duel.

lines.speaker: cornelia
lines.text: Rosalind!

lines.speaker: rosalind
lines.text: Over the soup, dear. Entirely over the soup.

lines.speaker: hugo
lines.text: A camphor chest lined with lead! Anjali, you'll have to forgive me, I'm going to stand very still and admire the joinery.

lines.speaker: anjali
lines.text: Open it, Hugo. My hands are shaking.

lines.speaker: hugo
lines.text: Lead lining, three layers of oiled silk, and a tin scoop. That's four hundred and sixty-two cups' worth.

lines.speaker: anjali
lines.text: The Society's tea. The last chest from the Wanderer's final voyage. We drank all but this.

lines.speaker: aldous
lines.text: I hope you will brew a cup for the Society, Anjali. It is a long time since we all had the same thing in our hands.

lines.speaker: mark
lines.text: The thirteenth tusk! It's, um, a pair with the twelfth, and they're holding up a door.

lines.speaker: prudence
lines.text: At last. The thinner dust in the bracket. I knew the Index was telling the truth.

lines.speaker: barnaby
lines.text: They're like a pair of curved gateposts, and they're holding up a little iron door, with a lock shaped like a crab!

lines.speaker: sam
lines.text: Another lock, another key. I begin to feel like a man in a very elaborate reading list.

lines.speaker: cornelia
lines.text: We have the crab key from the Archives. Mr Vane, if you would be so kind as to stand aside.

lines.speaker: zephyrine
lines.text: Spiral stair, iron rail, a long dark drop. I have been down it three times, Barnaby, and each time I came back up with a better story.

lines.speaker: barnaby
lines.text: This time I'd like to come back up with just myself.

lines.speaker: hugo
lines.text: I'll go first. I've tested every rivet. And I've put a little oil on the rail so it doesn't squeak.

lines.speaker: sam
lines.text: How very considerate, Hugo. You have made a spiral staircase polite.

lines.speaker: aldous
lines.text: And I shall go last, to count the steps, and to bring up the rear of any unfortunate descent.

lines.speaker: aldous
lines.text: Spiders! The loveliest web I have seen since Patagonia. Look at the silver on it, Mark, and look how it sways.

lines.speaker: mark
lines.text: She's called, um, Madame Archimedes. I've been feeding her. She's lonely, I think.

lines.speaker: rosalind
lines.text: A web with a chandelier's ambitions. I shall paint her in blue and silver, with the dew as pearls.

lines.speaker: barnaby
lines.text: She's looking right at me, Miss Thorne. All eight eyes.

lines.speaker: rosalind
lines.text: That means she approves, Barnaby. Spiders only stare at those they like.

lines.speaker: prudence
lines.text: Books! Grown all over with mushrooms in every colour of the rainbow, and not one of them damp. I'm in love.

lines.speaker: anjali
lines.text: The gold ones are chanterelles. The blue ones I'd leave alone. And the purple are, I think, only very shy.

lines.speaker: mark
lines.text: They've been growing for years, Anjali. I think the spores keep the paper dry, somehow.

lines.speaker: prudence
lines.text: Which means the library is protected, not decaying. Mark, you have made the most important discovery of the month.

lines.speaker: mark
lines.text: I didn't discover it, Prudence. I only stood still next to it.

lines.speaker: zephyrine
lines.text: The pool does not reflect the ceiling. It reflects a deck, and a lantern, and a very large sea.

lines.speaker: barnaby
lines.text: Miss Blackwood, there's a ship in it.

lines.speaker: zephyrine
lines.text: The Meridian, Barnaby. Every lamp lit, no one on the deck. A cup of tea on the captain's table, steaming.

lines.speaker: cornelia
lines.text: Is the cup full?

lines.speaker: zephyrine
lines.text: It is half full, Cornelia. As though somebody had put it down, only a moment ago, and meant to come back.

lines.speaker: aldous
lines.text: The Phantom Lantern has no flame, and no wick, and no shadow, and yet I can read my notes by it quite well.

lines.speaker: hugo
lines.text: It's cold, too. I held my hand against the glass. Not warm in the slightest.

lines.speaker: rosalind
lines.text: It is a light that is not for seeing by. It is for being seen by, I think.

lines.speaker: sam
lines.text: By whom, Rosalind?

lines.speaker: rosalind
lines.text: By anyone who is lost in the dark, and wondering which way is home.

lines.speaker: barnaby
lines.text: It's still warm, Miss Wren! The pillow, the quilt, even the little tin cup!

lines.speaker: anjali
lines.text: And a long grey hair, as soft as silk. Cornelia, it belongs to a very well-fed cat.

lines.speaker: cornelia
lines.text: A cat with a bed, a hat, a key, and a ham habit. Mr Pluck, kindly leave a saucer of milk.

lines.speaker: barnaby
lines.text: And a note! I'll write it. Dear Cat. Thank you for looking after the Vaults. Yours, Barnaby.

lines.speaker: zephyrine
lines.text: I have received less courteous correspondence from kings.

lines.speaker: hugo
lines.text: The casket has three tumblers. Each one wants a note from the lullaby, and the lullaby's in my head.

lines.speaker: zephyrine
lines.text: The sixth, the third, and the ninth. I tell you, Hugo, it is the order of the stars in the Dome.

lines.speaker: hugo
lines.text: Click. Click. Click. It's turning, Cornelia!

lines.speaker: cornelia
lines.text: It is a key. A single long brass key, and a wooden tag in a hand that I know. For the Founder's Study.

lines.speaker: prudence
lines.text: Mr Bloom, a hush, please. I believe the Hall has just spoken.

lines.speaker: cornelia
lines.text: The Rocking Chair. A small wooden chair on curved runners, with a faded blue cushion. It is an old friend of mine, and I did not know that it would be here.

lines.speaker: barnaby
lines.text: Miss Wren, you're crying.

lines.speaker: cornelia
lines.text: I am not crying, Mr Pluck. I have a very small speck in my eye.

lines.speaker: rosalind
lines.text: Cornelia. There is a name scratched into the arm. C. W., and a year. Do you remember?

lines.speaker: cornelia
lines.text: I remember. I was seven. Ambrose Hall found me on the steps of the Hall, in the rain, and he said that the Society would need a very good curator, someday. I have never forgotten it.

lines.speaker: cornelia
lines.text: The Old Wardrobe. Dark oak, with a brass key in the door, and a faint smell of mothballs and tea.

lines.speaker: barnaby
lines.text: I'll look inside, Miss Wren!

lines.speaker: cornelia
lines.text: Mr Pluck, I am quite sure it is only a wardrobe.

lines.speaker: barnaby
lines.text: It's got coats in it, and a hat, and a very small door at the back. I think there's a, hang on, there's a draught, it's very cold...

lines.speaker: cornelia
lines.text: Mr Pluck, come out at once.

lines.speaker: barnaby
lines.text: It's snowing in here, Miss Wren! In a wardrobe! It's gone!

lines.speaker: cornelia
lines.text: Barnaby!

lines.speaker: barnaby
lines.text: I'm back, Miss Wren. It was only a very small snow. And a lamp-post. I'll tell you later.

lines.speaker: rosalind
lines.text: The Rusted Birdbath Fountain. A stone basin, green with moss and orange with rust, and a little brass bird perched on the rim.

lines.speaker: aldous
lines.text: A wren! A little brass wren. Cornelia, it is you.

lines.speaker: cornelia
lines.text: Professor, it is a wren. A great many things in this Hall are wrens. It is not a personal matter.

lines.speaker: aldous
lines.text: It was a gift, Cornelia. The founder had it made for you, when you came to the Hall. It sang, I believe, when you filled the basin.

lines.speaker: cornelia
lines.text: Mr Pemberton, would you be so kind as to make it sing?

lines.speaker: hugo
lines.text: It'll take a day. And a little oil. And, I think, your patience.

lines.speaker: cornelia
lines.text: The Wing's Heart. A small, sunlit room, with a child's bed, a window seat, and a shelf of picture books. It is just as I left it.

lines.speaker: rosalind
lines.text: Cornelia, it is all right. You may sit down.

lines.speaker: cornelia
lines.text: I was the youngest member of the Society, Rosalind. For eleven years. And on the day he vanished, I stopped being a child. I stood in the Atrium, and I took the keys.

lines.speaker: sam
lines.text: You have kept this wing closed for twenty years.

lines.speaker: cornelia
lines.text: I could not bear to open it, Mr Vane. But now I find that I can. And I find that it is very kind to me. As if it had been waiting.

lines.speaker: barnaby
lines.text: Miss Wren, there's a picture book on the shelf. It's got your name on the cover. And inside, he's drawn a little map, to the Study.

lines.speaker: cornelia
lines.text: The Specimen Drawer Chest. Forty shallow drawers, each with a brass handle and a little card. I hardly dare to open them.

lines.speaker: aldous
lines.text: May I, Cornelia? I know how to open a drawer.

lines.speaker: cornelia
lines.text: You may open one, Professor. The one marked W.

lines.speaker: aldous
lines.text: It is a feather. A single wren's feather, and a note. Cornelia. Brave. Stubborn. Loves the Hall more than she will say. Keep her.

lines.speaker: cornelia
lines.text: Professor, I would prefer it if you did not read that aloud.

lines.speaker: aldous
lines.text: Oh dear. I already have. I am so sorry, my dear. I do tend to.

lines.speaker: sam
lines.text: The Drinks Tantalus. A locked oak stand, with three crystal decanters and a little silver key.

lines.speaker: cornelia
lines.text: Mr Vane, you are not to touch the decanters.

lines.speaker: sam
lines.text: Cornelia, I would not dream of it. I only wish to examine the key.

lines.speaker: rosalind
lines.text: Sam, the key is in your pocket.

lines.speaker: sam
lines.text: So it is. I must have put it there while I was thinking about something else.

lines.speaker: cornelia
lines.text: You are quite the worst thief in the Society, Mr Vane. You are very nearly the best of us.

lines.speaker: prudence
lines.text: The Study Bookcase. Six hundred volumes, every one of them annotated in pencil. I would know that handwriting anywhere.

lines.speaker: cornelia
lines.text: Is that, then, the founder's hand?

lines.speaker: prudence
lines.text: It is, Cornelia. And it is the most bewildering hand I have ever had the pleasure to catalogue. Notes on notes on notes, with arrows between them, and, in every margin, a tiny drawing of a clock.

lines.speaker: hugo
lines.text: Every margin, Prudence?

lines.speaker: prudence
lines.text: Every one. Even the dictionary. Under the word Time, he has drawn a clock that has stopped at a quarter to twelve.

lines.speaker: aldous
lines.text: The Vault Clock, as well. It has been saying the same thing for twenty years.

lines.speaker: hugo
lines.text: The Fossil Paperweights! Twelve little ammonites, each one set on a brass base, and each one holding down a very important sheet of paper.

lines.speaker: barnaby
lines.text: The papers are all blank, Hugo!

lines.speaker: hugo
lines.text: They're not blank, Barnaby. They've got writing in lemon juice. Hold it up to the lamp.

lines.speaker: zephyrine
lines.text: It is a list. Of places. Every one of them an island that is not on the map, and every one of them crossed out. Except the last.

lines.speaker: cornelia
lines.text: What is the last, Miss Blackwood?

lines.speaker: zephyrine
lines.text: Home. And beside it, in a very small hand: Not yet. Not quite.

lines.speaker: rosalind
lines.text: The Mounted Antlers. A grand pair of stag's horns, hung over the fireplace, and every one of the tines is a coat hook.

lines.speaker: barnaby
lines.text: There's a muffler on the top one, Miss Thorne! And a pair of gloves! And, oh, a hat!

lines.speaker: rosalind
lines.text: It is his, Barnaby. His muffler, his gloves, and his second-best hat. I gave him the muffler for his fiftieth birthday, and he wore it every single day, to the great alarm of the Society.

lines.speaker: cornelia
lines.text: It is a warm muffler. Someone has been wearing it, Miss Thorne. Very recently.

lines.speaker: rosalind
lines.text: I know, my dear. I am trying very hard to be sensible about it.

lines.speaker: cornelia
lines.text: The Founder's Unfinished Letter. A single sheet, half written, on the desk. The ink is still wet. It is addressed to the Society.

lines.speaker: sam
lines.text: Cornelia, it is wet. It cannot be. It has been twenty years.

lines.speaker: cornelia
lines.text: The ink has been wet for twenty years, Mr Vane. I think that is the whole point.

lines.speaker: rosalind
lines.text: Read it, Cornelia. Please. I do not trust myself.

lines.speaker: cornelia
lines.text: It says: My dear friends. If the Hall is awake, you have done what I could not. The Hall was built to keep the things that are lost, and the people who are lost with them. I went to find the last of them, and I will be home in time for, and then the sentence stops.

lines.speaker: prudence
lines.text: In time for what, Cornelia?

lines.speaker: cornelia
lines.text: It does not say, Miss Quill. But I rather think it ends with the word Wednesday.

lines.speaker: barnaby
lines.text: Miss Wren, I put my shoulder to the suit of armour and it swung round on a pin like a door!

lines.speaker: hugo
lines.text: A pivoting suit! No hinges to give it away. Whoever built it had a fine sense of mischief.

lines.speaker: prudence
lines.text: The Index lists a Passage, one line only. See also: Wall.

lines.speaker: cornelia
lines.text: It is a very short entry for such a long corridor. Come along, and do bring the lantern.

lines.speaker: sam
lines.text: I have been looking for this passage for thirty years, and I have walked into it in four minutes. I find I am offended.

lines.speaker: anjali
lines.text: Forty bells, each one labelled with a room, and the one marked Tea Room is ringing for two cups.

lines.speaker: barnaby
lines.text: I'll go, Miss Bose! I'll take the biscuits!

lines.speaker: cornelia
lines.text: Mr Pluck, you will take Mr Pemberton, and you will not eat them on the way.

lines.speaker: hugo
lines.text: Fine by me. If someone's ringing, I'll tell them the Tea Room's closed for refurbishment.

lines.speaker: anjali
lines.text: Go and look, both of you. And if there is a visitor, they are to be given the best chair and the best lemon cake.

lines.speaker: mark
lines.text: There's a tin of candles, and, um, a note on the lid. In case of darkness, light one. In case of light, light two.

lines.speaker: zephyrine
lines.text: Light two, then, and we shall see what the passage thinks of it.

lines.speaker: aldous
lines.text: It thinks, I believe, that a corridor which has not seen light in twenty years deserves a little extra.

lines.speaker: anjali
lines.text: It has also got longer, has it not? We have walked for twenty minutes, and I can still see the armour.

lines.speaker: mark
lines.text: Oh. Um. I think the passage has been, um, moving.

lines.speaker: barnaby
lines.text: I slid down the Spiral Newel Post, Miss Wren, and I'm very sorry, and I've lost a button.

lines.speaker: hugo
lines.text: Barnaby, stop. Put your hand on the post. It's turning.

lines.speaker: prudence
lines.text: The staircase is wound by those who use it. Every step we take is winding something above us.

lines.speaker: rosalind
lines.text: How very Ambrose. A house that is powered by the people who love it.

lines.speaker: cornelia
lines.text: Then the whole Hall is a clockwork, Mr Pemberton, and we are all part of the mechanism.

lines.speaker: mark
lines.text: Forty-two bats, hanging from the ledge, and every one of them asleep. They look like a row of very old bankers.

lines.speaker: aldous
lines.text: Mark, that is exactly right. I shall steal it for my next lecture.

lines.speaker: sam
lines.text: I have met bankers who looked like bats. It is a kinder comparison for the bats.

lines.speaker: barnaby
lines.text: I'm not breathing, Professor. In case they wake up and think I'm a very large moth.

lines.speaker: aldous
lines.text: Nonsense, my boy. A moth would be more graceful.

lines.speaker: zephyrine
lines.text: The stool is worn smooth by two hundred years of people waiting. I think I'll sit on it for a moment.

lines.speaker: cornelia
lines.text: Miss Blackwood, if you vanish, I shall take it personally.

lines.speaker: zephyrine
lines.text: I shan't vanish, Cornelia. I merely like to see what the watchman saw. Down this corridor, with his lamp, and his thoughts.

lines.speaker: sam
lines.text: And what did he see?

lines.speaker: zephyrine
lines.text: A door. And the door had a wren on it. I think we shall have to find it soon.

lines.speaker: prudence
lines.text: A secret reader's chair. A deep green armchair, a footstool, a candle-holder at the elbow, and a shelf of small and treasonable novels.

lines.speaker: rosalind
lines.text: Prudence, you are blushing. I do not think I have ever seen it.

lines.speaker: prudence
lines.text: I am not blushing. It is the candlelight. And the novels are, I'm told, entirely educational.

lines.speaker: sam
lines.text: One of them is called The Countess and the Cabin Boy. I should like to be educated.

lines.speaker: prudence
lines.text: Mr Vane, put that back at once.

lines.speaker: hugo
lines.text: It doesn't strike, doesn't chime, doesn't even tick loudly. It just keeps the time. And it says a quarter to twelve.

lines.speaker: aldous
lines.text: The fourth clock, Hugo. All of them agree. All of them are waiting.

lines.speaker: anjali
lines.text: For what? I would like to be told what we are waiting for, so I can put the kettle on in good time.

lines.speaker: hugo
lines.text: It's not waiting for midnight, Anjali. It's a quarter to twelve in the morning. It's waiting for noon.

lines.speaker: cornelia
lines.text: Noon, on a Wednesday, I suppose. I begin to dislike that day on principle.

lines.speaker: barnaby
lines.text: A basket with a cushion, a tiny hat on a peg, and, oh! She's in it! She's looking at me!

lines.speaker: anjali
lines.text: Grey, with a white chin and whiskers like a sea captain. And a key on a ribbon round her neck.

lines.speaker: cornelia
lines.text: Good afternoon. You must be the housekeeper.

lines.speaker: barnaby
lines.text: Her tag says Wednesday! She's Wednesday! She's been Wednesday all along!

lines.speaker: aldous
lines.text: Splendid. A Wednesday that has been watching over us for twenty years, and has never once been late.

lines.speaker: prudence
lines.text: A night light, Cornelia. The Index says it was lit every evening, at dusk, whether anyone was home or not.

lines.speaker: cornelia
lines.text: Why would a man leave a lamp lit in an empty passage?

lines.speaker: prudence
lines.text: So that if he ever came back in the dark, he would not trip over the cat.

lines.speaker: rosalind
lines.text: Oh, my dears, it is so very like him. A light, an open door, and a cat. And a great many clues, because he never could resist a puzzle.

lines.speaker: cornelia
lines.text: And a great deal of irritation for the rest of us, Rosalind.

lines.speaker: zephyrine
lines.text: I have used a bell like this on a mountain in Persia, to call a council. Everyone stops talking, and listens.

lines.speaker: hugo
lines.text: Does it work, Zephyrine? Really?

lines.speaker: zephyrine
lines.text: Ring it, Hugo.

lines.speaker: hugo
lines.text: I can't hear a thing. I mean, I can't hear myself think. It's wonderful.

lines.speaker: cornelia
lines.text: Then it shall live on my desk, Mr Pemberton, and it shall be rung at every committee meeting.

lines.speaker: aldous
lines.text: A single candle on the hidden stair. It burns an inch a night, and every morning it is an inch taller.

lines.speaker: hugo
lines.text: That's a wick on a spring, Professor. Clever work, with a little reservoir of wax in the base.

lines.speaker: mark
lines.text: I think it's lovely. Whoever made it wanted somebody to have a light, every night.

lines.speaker: barnaby
lines.text: But who's it for, Mr Bloom? Nobody's been down this stair in twenty years.

lines.speaker: mark
lines.text: Somebody has. The wax on the step is a few hours old.

lines.speaker: rosalind
lines.text: Draw the curtain, put the lamp behind it, and we shall have a performance! Barnaby, you shall be the rabbit.

lines.speaker: barnaby
lines.text: I can do a rabbit, and a dove, and, er, a very bad dog.

lines.speaker: sam
lines.text: Allow me. This is a swan, of a rather brooding disposition.

lines.speaker: anjali
lines.text: Sam, that is a lobster.

lines.speaker: sam
lines.text: Anjali, it is a swan in a lobster's mood. Rosalind, you must paint me on the screen.

lines.speaker: rosalind
lines.text: You are already there, darling. Do not move.

lines.speaker: hugo
lines.text: A ring of sixteen lanterns turning very slowly overhead. That's the light for a very important room, Cornelia.

lines.speaker: cornelia
lines.text: Miss Quill, do we have a plan of the Chamber?

lines.speaker: prudence
lines.text: We have a single line. Chamber: see Dome. And a drawing of a roof, but without any building under it.

lines.speaker: zephyrine
lines.text: A Dome with no room beneath it. Or a room with no roof above.

lines.speaker: barnaby
lines.text: There's a bit of painted plaster in the next passage, Miss Blackwood. It's leaning on a cabinet. It looks like stars.

lines.speaker: rosalind
lines.text: That is my sky. I painted it for him, the winter before he left. Every star, in gold leaf.

lines.speaker: zephyrine
lines.text: It is the edge of the chart, Rosalind. I know that sky. I saw it from the stern of the Meridian.

lines.speaker: rosalind
lines.text: He told me it was a map, and I thought he was being charming.

lines.speaker: cornelia
lines.text: A map of what, Rosalind?

lines.speaker: rosalind
lines.text: Of the ceiling of the Chamber, my dear. A roof for a room that has not been built yet, because he ran out of time.

lines.speaker: barnaby
lines.text: I pumped the bellows and the whole wall began to sing, Miss Wren!

lines.speaker: hugo
lines.text: It's an organ pipe, built into the stonework. Same lullaby, a little flat.

lines.speaker: aldous
lines.text: Flat, Hugo? It sounds to me like somebody trying to hum along, and not quite finding the note.

lines.speaker: mark
lines.text: Then we should help it. Together, on the sixth.

lines.speaker: cornelia
lines.text: All of you, please. I shall conduct. Do not look at me. Look at the pipes.

lines.speaker: prudence
lines.text: A hundred rolled blueprints, tied with ribbon, and every one is for a wing of the Hall.

lines.speaker: hugo
lines.text: The Gasworks, the Orrery, the pipes. All his own sketches. And the last tube, Prudence, is it sealed?

lines.speaker: prudence
lines.text: It is. And inside is a plan of the Hall seen from above, and it is not a building at all. It is a ship.

lines.speaker: cornelia
lines.text: The Clock Tower is the mast, and every wing a deck. And she is riding at anchor, waiting for a crew.

lines.speaker: aldous
lines.text: A ship! That explains the flag on the Relief Model. And the stairs. And the creaking.

lines.speaker: sam
lines.text: A throne, Cornelia, and it is plainly meant for you. I propose a toast.

lines.speaker: cornelia
lines.text: I do not wish to sit on a throne, Mr Vane.

lines.speaker: rosalind
lines.text: It is not a throne, my dear. The Society has no president. It has a chair, and the chair is for whoever minds the Hall best.

lines.speaker: anjali
lines.text: Then it has been waiting for you since the first morning, and I shall bring a cushion.

lines.speaker: cornelia
lines.text: If I sit in it, I shall sit only to tell you that I told you so.

lines.speaker: rosalind
lines.text: And now I may tell you what the Hall was for. It was for finding what was lost. Including a girl on the steps.

lines.speaker: cornelia
lines.text: A door of iron and oak, with a keyhole in the shape of a wren. I should like a moment alone with it, please.

lines.speaker: barnaby
lines.text: I'll stand guard, Miss Wren! Nobody gets past me, except you!

lines.speaker: zephyrine
lines.text: The key that was under the feather, Cornelia, in drawer W. It was never for the Study at all.

lines.speaker: hugo
lines.text: It's not a lock, it's a promise. Look at the wards. They've been cut to fit one particular key, and one particular hand.

lines.speaker: cornelia
lines.text: Then I shall turn it myself. Behind this door, I think, is a great many maps, and a great deal of the truth.

lines.speaker: zephyrine
lines.text: The Star Fixing Table! A great round table of black glass, ruled with silver lines, for plotting the position of the stars.

lines.speaker: cornelia
lines.text: Miss Blackwood, you look like a woman who has come home.

lines.speaker: zephyrine
lines.text: I do, rather. I spent more evenings at a table like this than I did in any bed. Every star I ever measured is a friend, and every one of them is on this glass.

lines.speaker: sam
lines.text: Zephyrine, you have not mentioned that you are an astronomer.

lines.speaker: zephyrine
lines.text: I am a cartographer, Sam. An astronomer is a cartographer who has given up on the ground.

lines.speaker: hugo
lines.text: The Chart Room Clock! A tall case clock, as thin as a spar, with a face as clear as the moon. It says a quarter to twelve. I wondered when we should come to it.

lines.speaker: aldous
lines.text: The fifth clock, Hugo. And it is, I believe, the one that tells the others what to do.

lines.speaker: hugo
lines.text: It's got a pendulum with a window in it. Look. There's a tiny brass ship, swinging back and forth.

lines.speaker: cornelia
lines.text: The Meridian.

lines.speaker: hugo
lines.text: She's been swinging for twenty years, Cornelia. And every swing, she gets a little closer to the shore.

lines.speaker: zephyrine
lines.text: The Polar Map Table! The whole of the White North, in embossed leather and polished ivory. I have walked across half of it.

lines.speaker: anjali
lines.text: And I have cooked on the other half. I have a recipe for seal that I will take to my grave.

lines.speaker: zephyrine
lines.text: Anjali, please do not take it to the grave. I should like to try it, in the right circumstances.

lines.speaker: sam
lines.text: I should like to try it in any circumstances, as long as there is a decent bottle of claret.

lines.speaker: cornelia
lines.text: I note that the table has a hand-drawn arrow pointing at a spot just off the edge, labelled: Here.

lines.speaker: prudence
lines.text: The Lost Maps Cabinet. Eighty drawers, each with a map of a place that has never been found. Every one of them labelled, and every one of them in order.

lines.speaker: zephyrine
lines.text: Prudence, this is the loveliest thing I have ever seen. Every one of these is a place that someone once believed in.

lines.speaker: prudence
lines.text: There is a drawer for the last of them, Zephyrine, and it is empty. The label says: The Hall.

lines.speaker: cornelia
lines.text: Then the Hall is the last of the lost places. And we are in it.

lines.speaker: prudence
lines.text: It is rather a tidy thought, Cornelia. I do not know whether I find it comforting, or merely complete.

lines.speaker: rosalind
lines.text: The Cartographer's Easel! A tall oak frame, with a great sheet of paper stretched across it, and a box of fine brushes. I should like to draw the whole Hall, from the Gates to the Tower.

lines.speaker: zephyrine
lines.text: Rosalind, you will draw it as you see it. I will draw it as I know it. We will see where they differ.

lines.speaker: rosalind
lines.text: They will differ in every particular, my dear, and I can think of nothing I should rather do.

lines.speaker: mark
lines.text: I'll mix the colours, Miss Thorne. I'd like to, um, get the green right.

lines.speaker: rosalind
lines.text: Mark, that is the first time I have heard you volunteer for anything. I accept, with pleasure.

lines.speaker: cornelia
lines.text: The Explorer's Table. A long, scarred oak table with a lamp at each end and a place laid for every member of the Society. The cups are warm.

lines.speaker: barnaby
lines.text: Miss Wren, there's a place for me! There's a cup with my name on it!

lines.speaker: cornelia
lines.text: There is a place for everybody, Mr Pluck. Including the cat.

lines.speaker: barnaby
lines.text: There's a saucer by the cat's place, and it's got milk in it, and it's still warm. Somebody put it there this morning!

lines.speaker: sam
lines.text: Cornelia, I have been in a great many strange rooms. I have never been in one where the tea is warm and there is nobody to be seen.

lines.speaker: cornelia
lines.text: It is a very polite sort of haunting, Mr Vane. I would not like to disturb it.

lines.speaker: zephyrine
lines.text: The Map of Everything! A great chart that covers the whole wall, from floor to ceiling, and every line on it has been drawn in a different hand.

lines.speaker: cornelia
lines.text: It is the Society's own map of the world. And, in the centre, a small cross. Here.

lines.speaker: zephyrine
lines.text: The Hall. And a line running from it, a long red line, off the edge of the paper and on to the wall. To the Clock Tower.

lines.speaker: prudence
lines.text: It is a route, Cornelia. And it is dated, in every stage. A Wednesday in March. A Wednesday in April. A Wednesday in May. Every week for twenty years.

lines.speaker: cornelia
lines.text: He has been coming back every Wednesday. And we have not been here to meet him.

lines.speaker: barnaby
lines.text: Miss Wren, I've counted on my cuff. It's Wednesday today, again.

lines.speaker: sam
lines.text: The Ballroom Mirror Panel! A great sheet of silvered glass, framed in gilt, and reflecting an entire floor of waxed oak. I look splendid in it.

lines.speaker: rosalind
lines.text: Sam, you look exactly the same as you did at twenty. A little more varnished.

lines.speaker: sam
lines.text: Rosalind, I shall treasure that. As a compliment, I think.

lines.speaker: cornelia
lines.text: The Grand Ballroom is the last great room of the Hall. The League has a card on the table. They wish to attend our reopening gala.

lines.speaker: anjali
lines.text: We shall invite them. We shall feed them. And we shall make them feel that they have never been so welcome in their lives.

lines.speaker: cornelia
lines.text: Miss Bose, that is the most dangerous kind of hospitality.

lines.speaker: hugo
lines.text: The Dancing Master's Cane! A tall black stick with a silver knob, for tapping out the beat. It's got a lovely weight.

lines.speaker: barnaby
lines.text: Hugo, can you waltz?

lines.speaker: hugo
lines.text: I can polka, Barnaby. It's a different thing. It's mostly a question of tempo and not looking down.

lines.speaker: barnaby
lines.text: I can't polka. I can only fall over in time.

lines.speaker: aldous
lines.text: That is the first principle of the waltz, Barnaby. It is merely falling over in a very graceful circle.

lines.speaker: rosalind
lines.text: Come, my dears. We shall have lessons on Thursday, in the Ballroom, and everyone shall be bad at it together.

lines.speaker: prudence
lines.text: The Opera Glasses Stand. A row of little brass binoculars on a velvet rail, each one with a mother-of-pearl handle. I recommend them for observing the Society.

lines.speaker: cornelia
lines.text: I have used them for years, Miss Quill. They are good for watching people who think they are not being watched.

lines.speaker: prudence
lines.text: I see Mr Merrick, in the gallery, wearing a green carnation and a very tight smile.

lines.speaker: sam
lines.text: He is always in the gallery, Prudence. It is the best seat, and the cheapest.

lines.speaker: cornelia
lines.text: Do not look, but he is looking at us. And, I think, at the founder's portrait.

lines.speaker: mark
lines.text: The Floral Centrepiece! A great arrangement of white roses, ivory lilies, and, um, the flower from the edge of the map. In a silver bowl, as big as a cartwheel.

lines.speaker: rosalind
lines.text: Mark, you have outdone yourself. It is the loveliest thing I have seen in a ballroom. And, I should say, quite as tall as I am.

lines.speaker: mark
lines.text: It, um, wasn't just me. Mr Pluck held the ladder, and Anjali held the vase, and Hugo held the, um, the bolts.

lines.speaker: anjali
lines.text: And I held my tongue, Mark. Which is the greatest feat of all.

lines.speaker: cornelia
lines.text: The Society has done it together. I do not think I have ever been so proud of a flower.

lines.speaker: hugo
lines.text: The Bandleader's Podium! A little round platform, with a brass rail and a music stand. I'm to conduct, Cornelia.

lines.speaker: cornelia
lines.text: Mr Pemberton, you cannot conduct. You cannot even read music.

lines.speaker: hugo
lines.text: I can read the lullaby, Cornelia. It's the only tune in the Hall. We'll play it as a waltz.

lines.speaker: zephyrine
lines.text: A waltz in six-eight, with the sixth note held. Hugo, that is genius.

lines.speaker: hugo
lines.text: I know. I'm as surprised as you are. I think the Hall's been teaching me, and I haven't noticed.

lines.speaker: barnaby
lines.text: Miss Wren, there's a man at the door in a green carnation.

lines.speaker: rosalind
lines.text: The Cut Glass Chandelier! Four thousand crystals, hung in nine tiers, all blazing. It is the finest thing in the Ballroom, and the finest thing I have ever seen in a ceiling.

lines.speaker: cornelia
lines.text: Mr Merrick has just arrived. He is in the doorway, looking up.

lines.speaker: sam
lines.text: He is looking at the chandelier, Cornelia. And then at the clock. And then at the door to the Tower.

lines.speaker: cornelia
lines.text: He knows the Tower is the thing. I wonder what else he knows.

lines.speaker: sam
lines.text: That the founder will return, Cornelia. And that he will be the first to find him. It is what the League has been planning for twenty years.

lines.speaker: cornelia
lines.text: Then they shall have the pleasure of waiting, as we have.

lines.speaker: cornelia
lines.text: The Last Dance Slippers. A pair of little silk shoes, white as snow, and worn very slightly at the toe. I have wanted to dance in them since I was seven.

lines.speaker: rosalind
lines.text: Then dance, Cornelia. Here, with all of us, before the League and the whole Society.

lines.speaker: cornelia
lines.text: Mr Merrick, I have a proposal. The League may attend our gala, take our tea, and sit in our chairs. In return, you will sign the Charter, and agree to be a member like any other.

lines.speaker: sam
lines.text: Lucian, I should take it. I have found, in my experience, that membership is a great deal more fun than ownership.

lines.speaker: aldous
lines.text: Splendid! A man who signs the Charter is a man who must also dance. And I should like to see it.

lines.speaker: barnaby
lines.text: He's signing it, Miss Wren! He's signed it! He's in!

lines.speaker: cornelia
lines.text: Then the League has been dissolved, and the Society restored. Play the waltz, Mr Pemberton.

lines.speaker: aldous
lines.text: The Pigeon Perch! A little ledge, high on the north face of the Tower, with a hundred little holes, and a hundred pigeons.

lines.speaker: barnaby
lines.text: They're all looking at me, Professor.

lines.speaker: aldous
lines.text: They are looking at the crumbs in your pocket, Barnaby. You have been giving them biscuits.

lines.speaker: barnaby
lines.text: I have not! Only a few. Only the ones with raisins.

lines.speaker: cornelia
lines.text: Mr Pluck, the Hall is a place of rules. Biscuits are not for pigeons.

lines.speaker: aldous
lines.text: Cornelia, every great Hall in the world has had its pigeons. And every great Hall in the world has made its peace with them.

lines.speaker: hugo
lines.text: The Clock Mechanic's Chair! A stool on a spindle, with a toolbox in a leather satchel, and a spanner in the shape of a seahorse. This is the best chair I've ever seen.

lines.speaker: cornelia
lines.text: It is yours, Mr Pemberton. I think it has been waiting for you.

lines.speaker: hugo
lines.text: I feel as if I've sat in it before. I know where everything is. I could close my eyes, and put my hand on the right screw.

lines.speaker: aldous
lines.text: It is a very familiar sensation, Hugo. I have it all the time in the Hall of Feathers.

lines.speaker: hugo
lines.text: It's the hands, Aldous. They remember what the head forgets.

lines.speaker: zephyrine
lines.text: The Quarter Chimes! Five brass bells, in a row, each a different pitch. They ring every fifteen minutes, and they have not rung for twenty years.

lines.speaker: cornelia
lines.text: Mr Pemberton, are we ready?

lines.speaker: hugo
lines.text: We're ready, Cornelia. Barnaby, stand by the rope.

lines.speaker: barnaby
lines.text: Aye, Mr Pemberton! Five bells. Do-re-mi-fa-sol. Oh, listen! The whole Hall is chiming!

lines.speaker: rosalind
lines.text: It sounds like the Hall is waking up. For the last time, and the first.

lines.speaker: cornelia
lines.text: It is a quarter past eleven, Miss Thorne. We have forty-five minutes.

lines.speaker: aldous
lines.text: The Astronomical Clock Face. A great dial of blue enamel, with the sun and the moon in brass, and the constellations in silver. It tells the hour, the day, the month, and the position of the planets.

lines.speaker: hugo
lines.text: It's the most complicated clock I've ever had in my hands, Aldous. It's got more wheels than the Hall has rooms.

lines.speaker: zephyrine
lines.text: It is a map of the sky, and a map of the year, and a map of the day. And, I think, it is also a map of someone's heart.

lines.speaker: cornelia
lines.text: Miss Blackwood, do not be sentimental.

lines.speaker: zephyrine
lines.text: I am a cartographer, Cornelia. It is a form of sentiment. We just draw it better.

lines.speaker: hugo
lines.text: The Great Mainspring! A coil of steel as long as a rowing boat, wound in a spiral inside a brass drum. And it's wound, Cornelia. It's wound all the way.

lines.speaker: cornelia
lines.text: Do you mean that every step in the Hall has wound it, Mr Pemberton?

lines.speaker: hugo
lines.text: Every step. Every bit of tea carried up the stairs. Every door that opened. It's been waiting for us, and for twenty years, and it's now at full tension.

lines.speaker: prudence
lines.text: It is a quarter to twelve, Cornelia. By every clock in the Hall.

lines.speaker: cornelia
lines.text: Then we shall climb. All of us, together. And we shall see what the Dial has to say.

lines.speaker: cornelia
lines.text: The Great Clock Tower Dial. A face as large as a house, glowing in the midday sun. It is eleven fifty-nine, and the hands are about to meet.

lines.speaker: barnaby
lines.text: Miss Wren, I'm holding my breath.

lines.speaker: cornelia
lines.text: We all are, Mr Pluck. We have all been holding it for a great deal longer than twenty years.

lines.speaker: rosalind
lines.text: The big hand has met the little hand, my dears. It is noon.

lines.speaker: aldous
lines.text: The clock is striking! Twelve. And, oh, my goodness, a thirteenth!

lines.speaker: zephyrine
lines.text: And behind the dial, a door is opening. And on the other side, a staircase, and a very faint light. And a smell of tea.

lines.speaker: barnaby
lines.text: The Broken Rocking Horse! A beautiful dapple-grey horse, with a cracked leg and a missing ear. I could fix him in an afternoon.

lines.speaker: hugo
lines.text: I'll help, Barnaby. We'll make him as good as new. A new rocker, a bit of glue, and a very good ear.

lines.speaker: cornelia
lines.text: The Attic of Marvels. It is the last wing, and it is as dusty as the first.

lines.speaker: anjali
lines.text: I should like to bring up a pot of tea, and sit among the marvels for a week.

lines.speaker: cornelia
lines.text: You may, Miss Bose. But first, we must find what the founder left behind. Come, all of you. Be careful where you tread.

lines.speaker: rosalind
lines.text: The Magic Lantern Slides! A box of glass plates, painted with scenes of every place the founder ever visited. Hold one up to the light, and it glows.

lines.speaker: zephyrine
lines.text: It is a journey, Rosalind. Hold them in order. The Gates, the Atrium, the Library, the Deep Vaults, the Tower. And the last, a great white sea, and a small boat.

lines.speaker: aldous
lines.text: There is a figure standing in the boat. He is waving. And behind him, the Meridian, with all her lamps lit.

lines.speaker: cornelia
lines.text: He is not lost, Professor. Look at his face. He is exactly where he intended to be.

lines.speaker: barnaby
lines.text: And he's smiling, Miss Wren. He's smiling at us.

lines.speaker: prudence
lines.text: The Wishing Well Bucket. A little copper pail on a rope, at the bottom of a very deep well. At the bottom, a coin, and a folded note.

lines.speaker: cornelia
lines.text: Miss Quill, will you read it?

lines.speaker: prudence
lines.text: It says: Dear Cornelia. I wished, long ago, that you would have a Hall to come home to. I wished that you would not be alone. And I wished, most of all, that you would never need to find me.

lines.speaker: cornelia
lines.text: He wished that I would not need to find him. And yet we have all spent twenty years doing precisely that.

lines.speaker: rosalind
lines.text: Cornelia, my dear, that is exactly what it was for. A Hall is a place that is found, not a place that is left.

lines.speaker: sam
lines.text: Then I am found, I think. I have been, for some time.

lines.speaker: cornelia
lines.text: The Founder's Last Marvel. Every wing is restored, every room is lit, and every member is gathered. And on the table, a single, very small card.

lines.speaker: barnaby
lines.text: Miss Wren! It's addressed to everybody!

lines.speaker: cornelia
lines.text: It reads: Dear friends. The Hall is yours. Keep it as I could not. I have gone ahead to see what is next, and I shall be back by Wednesday.

lines.speaker: sam
lines.text: Which Wednesday?

lines.speaker: aldous
lines.text: He did not say, Sam. That is the whole joy of it.

lines.speaker: rosalind
lines.text: Then we shall wait, my dears. With the lamps lit, and the door unlocked, and the kettle on.

lines.speaker: cornelia
lines.text: And in the meantime, Mr Pluck, there is a very great deal of Hall to look after. Fetch the polish. Gently.

panels.caption: A weathered placard on the gates reads Curio Hall, By Appointment of the Society, and beneath it, in smaller letters, Do Wipe Your Boots. Beyond the ivy, a long gravel drive curves toward a great dark house, and one lit window.
Cornelia Wren has been holding the keys since the winter the founder disappeared. She hands them over now with a very straight back, and Barnaby Pluck carries the first lantern.
Behind the Atrium, a narrow vestibule smells of wet umbrellas and old wool. Hooks line the walls, and a barometer on the far panel has been stuck at Stormy since before anyone can remember.
panels.subject: a narrow Victorian museum vestibule smelling of damp wool: long rows of empty brass coat hooks along teal panelled walls, a few wet umbrellas dripping by the door, a round brass barometer on the far panel, warm gaslight, dusty and quiet, nobody in the room

panels.caption: Every cloakroom in the world has a secret, and this one has a hamper of hats nobody ever came back for.
panels.subject: inside a cloakroom, Cornelia Wren, an elderly formidable lady curator with silver-grey hair in a bun and a dark teal high-collared dress, and Barnaby Pluck, a cheerful clean-shaven young porter in a green waistcoat with rolled sleeves, lift the lid of a big wicker hamper overflowing with forgotten hats, gloves and scarves; teal panelled walls, brass coat hooks, warm gaslight

panels.caption: The Curator's Office sits at the top of a short flight of stairs, its door painted the green of old brass. Inside, a desk the size of a small boat faces a window that looks out over the entire Hall.
panels.subject: a Victorian curator's study at dusk seen from the door: a brass-green painted door standing open, an enormous mahogany partners' desk like a small boat facing a tall window that looks out over the rooftops of a great museum, warm lamplight, nobody in the room

panels.caption: One drawer of the desk sticks fast, and no one has dared to force it in twenty years.
panels.subject: close view of a big mahogany desk with one drawer shut tight, Cornelia Wren, an elderly formidable lady curator with silver-grey hair in a bun and a dark teal high-collared dress, studying it with arms folded while Professor Aldous Finch, a thin absent-minded elderly ornithologist in a rumpled tweed coat with binoculars round his neck, peers over her shoulder holding a field notebook; warm lamplight, walnut panelling

panels.caption: The Tea Room doors swing wide, and a smell of lemon, cardamom, and long-cold ashes drifts out. Every table is laid for four, as if the guests had only stepped out for a moment.
panels.subject: the doors of a Victorian tea room swing open on tables laid for four with white cloths, china cups and silver, an old samovar and cold ash in a hearth, lace-curtained windows at dusk, dust motes in warm light, nobody there

panels.caption: The Society runs on tea, as everyone knows. Without it, nothing in the Hall has quite the right temperature.
panels.subject: Cornelia Wren, an elderly formidable lady curator with silver-grey hair in a bun and a dark teal high-collared dress, and Barnaby Pluck, a cheerful clean-shaven young porter in a green waistcoat with rolled sleeves, stand in a Victorian tea room at a long table laid with a tea set; he holds up a teapot hopefully, she regards the room sternly; warm gaslight, cream and teal walls

panels.caption: The Hall of Feathers is a tall room full of whispering wings. Cases of sparrows, parrots, and a very surprised owl line the walls, and a great skylight pours down a column of pale gold.
panels.subject: a tall Victorian bird gallery with glass cases of sparrows, parrots and one startled-looking owl lining the walls, a great skylight pouring a column of pale gold light down the middle, grey feathers drifting in the air, nobody in the room

panels.caption: Somewhere in the rafters, something rustles that is not a mouse.
panels.subject: Cornelia Wren, an elderly formidable lady curator with silver-grey hair in a bun and a dark teal high-collared dress, and Professor Aldous Finch, a thin absent-minded elderly ornithologist in a rumpled tweed coat with binoculars round his neck, look up into the dark rafters of a tall bird gallery where something feathered rustles; a column of gold skylight, glass cases of stuffed birds, drifting feathers

panels.caption: The Butterfly House is built of glass and cast iron, and when the door opens a warm breath of damp earth and flowers rolls out. Pins gleam in the dark like a thousand small stars.
panels.subject: a Victorian butterfly house of glass and cast iron opening in the dusk, a warm breath of green foliage and damp earth, thousands of pinned butterflies gleaming like small stars in dark cases, soft lantern light, nobody in the room

panels.caption: No living butterfly has flown here in twenty years. Barnaby swears one landed on his hat.
panels.subject: Cornelia Wren, an elderly formidable lady curator with silver-grey hair in a bun and a dark teal high-collared dress, and Professor Aldous Finch, a thin absent-minded elderly ornithologist in a rumpled tweed coat with binoculars round his neck, stand inside a Victorian glasshouse full of ferns and pinned butterfly cases; one blue butterfly rests on the professor's hat and he is trying not to move; warm humid light

panels.caption: The Conservatory has grown wild. Ferns have pushed through the floor tiles, gourds drape the arches, and a pitcher plant the size of a hat has taken the best chair.
panels.subject: an overgrown Victorian conservatory: ferns pushed up through cracked floor tiles, striped gourds draped over iron arches, an enormous pitcher plant sitting on a wicker chair, glass dome above in evening light, nobody in the room

panels.caption: Someone has been misting the leaves. The droplets are fresh.
panels.subject: Cornelia Wren, an elderly formidable lady curator with silver-grey hair in a bun and a dark teal high-collared dress, and Sam Vane, a suave man in his thirties in a well-cut dark frock coat, stand among the ferns of an overgrown conservatory, touching glistening misted leaves in surprise; iron arches, evening light

panels.caption: Down a wide stone corridor, the Fossil Gallery opens like a ribcage. Pale bones rise into the shadows, and the floor is dusted with the grey powder of ancient stone.
panels.subject: a wide stone corridor opening into a Victorian fossil gallery shaped like a giant ribcage: pale curved bones rising into shadow, the floor dusted with grey stone powder, cool blue light, nobody in the room

panels.caption: Aldous Finch says it is the quietest room in the Hall. Barnaby says that is exactly why he does not like it.
panels.subject: Professor Aldous Finch, a thin absent-minded elderly ornithologist in a rumpled tweed coat with binoculars round his neck, and Barnaby Pluck, a cheerful clean-shaven young porter in a green waistcoat with rolled sleeves, walk uneasily through a hall of towering pale fossil bones, the young porter glancing nervously at the shadows while the professor smiles happily; grey dust on the floor

panels.caption: The Mineral Vault is lined with iron shelves and velvet drawers, and the lamplight catches in a hundred hidden crystals. At the far end, a round steel door the size of a cartwheel stands closed.
panels.subject: a Victorian mineral vault lined with iron shelves and velvet-lined drawers, lamplight catching in a hundred hidden crystals, and at the far end a round steel vault door the size of a cartwheel, closed, nobody in the room

panels.caption: Cornelia does not say what is behind it. She only says that the Society was very careful.
panels.subject: Cornelia Wren, an elderly formidable lady curator with silver-grey hair in a bun and a dark teal high-collared dress, stands before a huge round steel vault door with a spoked wheel handle, her hand resting on it gravely, while Barnaby Pluck, a cheerful clean-shaven young porter in a green waistcoat with rolled sleeves, waits behind her holding a lantern; dark vault, crystal glints

panels.caption: The Shell and Coral Room is cool and hushed, like the inside of a conch. Pearl-lined cases glow faintly in the dark, and somewhere very near, the sound of the sea is playing from a spiral shell.
It is the sort of room that makes one speak very quietly, and then not speak at all.

Green light ripples across the walls of the Aquarium Grotto. Great glass tanks, long empty, wait for the water to come back, and at the bottom of the largest one, something small and square is shining.
The light moves, and it seems, for a moment, that it is waving.
The Map Room is lined from floor to ceiling with charts, rolled and flat, pinned and framed. Every coast is inked in a different hand, and a great brass compass is sunk into the floor.
A single black pin sits in the middle of a map, with no thread attached to it at all.
The Library of Expeditions climbs three storeys, with iron galleries and a ladder on a rail. The books are shelved by voyage, and each voyage has its own colour of spine.
On the highest shelf, a single blue book sits slightly out of line, as if it had been put back in a hurry.
Rolling shelves fill the Archives, and every drawer is labelled in a tiny neat hand. Someone has been here in the dark, and everything has been refiled. Not one thing is where it was.
It smells of old paper, ink, and, very faintly, of ham sandwiches.
The Clockwork Workshop rattles with a faint, invisible ticking. Benches hold a thousand half-built wonders, and from the ceiling hang chains of cogs, like a mechanical orchard.
Every spring in the room is wound to precisely the right tension. Nobody has wound a thing in twenty years.
The Hall of Instruments gleams like a jeweller's window. Brass and glass line every wall: galvanometers, theodolites, a great seismograph with its needle trembling over a blank roll of paper.
Everything here measures something. Cornelia suspects it is measuring them.

A spiral stair climbs into the Astronomy Dome, and at the top the night sky wheels slowly overhead, painted on a great hemisphere of dark blue glass. Telescopes point in every direction, and one of them is pointing at the door.
The stars on the ceiling are in the right places. It is the first thing about the Hall that has been entirely reliable.
The Orrery Landing is a gallery of dusty planets. Moons hang from their wires, a banded giant sits sulking in the corner, and a comet sleeps in a case marked Do Not Wake.
The great orrery in the centre is missing its sun.
The Gaslight Gallery is a long hall of glass globes and brass pipes, and every lamp is out. Someone, long ago, filled every jet with a little oil, and then walked away.
When the first one is lit, it is as though the Hall draws in a long breath.

The Sculpture Court is a square of pale stone open to the sky, with a dry fountain at its heart and marble figures standing about in the leaves. One of them has lost its head, and another seems to be looking for it.
A stone bench sits against the far wall, and on it, someone has left a half-eaten apple.

The Hall of Giants soars over the visitor's head. A giraffe's neck disappears into the gloom, a pair of tusks curve like cathedral arches, and an enormous spider crab stretches across the floor like a mournful carpet.
A very small door is set into the base of one skeleton. It is, Barnaby decides, for mice.
The Insectarium hums with a thousand silent wings. Cases of beetles glitter like pirate treasure, and a great glass nest sits in the middle of the floor, quite empty, but not entirely quiet.
Everything here is very small and very well organised. The Hall approves.
The Herbarium smells of hay and sunlit paper. Pressed flowers are framed in their hundreds, and a long worktable is set with magnifiers, tweezers, and an enormous unfinished atlas.
A single page in the atlas has been left blank, with a little pressed flower beside it that no one can name.

The Apothecary Annex is a dark panelled room of tiny drawers, and every drawer is labelled in Latin. Bottles of every colour wait on the shelves, and a big brass bell sits on the counter, begging to be rung.
A faint sweet smell hangs over everything: sulphur, honey, and, strangely, mint.
The Gemstone Salon is lined with blue velvet, and the cases glitter in the light of a single lamp. Every stone has its place on a cushion of silk, and every place has its own little brass plate.
Sam Vane stands in the doorway for a very long time, with his hands very firmly in his pockets.
The Meteorite Chamber is a round room with a black floor, and the walls are hung with fragments of the sky. Some are warm to the touch. All of them are very, very old.
Zephyrine says that stones that have fallen from the sky always remember the way back up.
The Cabinet of Whispers is a narrow room of mahogany panels and curved brass horns. As the door closes, a hush falls, and then, very softly, from every wall, a murmur begins.
Nobody can make out the words. Everybody agrees that they were meant for somebody in particular.
A grand stair sweeps up from the Gallery, and every step is hung with portraits. Duchesses, explorers, and one very stern bishop watch the visitor climb. The last frame at the turn is empty.
The paintings are not looking at the visitor. They are all looking at the same spot on the stairs.

The Founders' Gallery is a long, quiet room, with a cold hearth at one end and a great window at the other. Nine chairs stand around a table of dark wood, and one of them is pulled back, as if someone had just risen.
On the table, a pen rests in an inkwell. The ink is still wet.
The Music Box Parlor is a little room of velvet and brass. Hundreds of music boxes stand in rows, each with a tiny key, and all of them are wound just enough to begin.
When the door closes, they all play the same lullaby, a little out of time. They have been waiting to be asked.

The Print and Poster Room smells of ink and hot lead. Wooden type fills every drawer, and old posters flap on a line like washing: A Talk on Larks, A Debate on the Moon, A Concert for Seventeen Triangles.
A great iron press crouches in the corner, still faintly warm.
The Model Ship Hall is a long vaulted space, with ships in bottles, ships on shelves, and a whole fleet in full sail across the floor. The ceiling is painted with a thousand little waves.
The place of honour at the centre of the fleet is empty, with a small brass plate: Meridian.
A ladder and a trapdoor lead up to the Balloon Loft, where silk billows in the rafters like sleeping clouds. Baskets are woven, burners polished, and a rope hangs out of the roof, down into the dark.
A launch deck juts into the evening sky. Barnaby does not look down.

The Observatory Walk runs along the roof of the Hall, with a stone balustrade, a row of lamps, and the whole night spread out like a sea. Telescopes stand on every corner, and every one is pointed at the same star.
It is a quiet, windy, wonderful place, and the birds have already found it.
The Moonlit Courtyard is a square of cool green in the middle of the Hall. A single old tree stands at the centre, and its leaves are silver in the moonlight.
The Hall is quiet here. It feels, for the first time, like a house with someone sleeping in it.
The Reflecting Pool is long and black and perfectly still, and it holds the sky as a plate holds a cake. At the far end, a stone fountain stands dry, and a small white boat is tied to a post.
Everything in the pool is a little different from what stands above it. A lantern is lit in the reflection that is not lit in the room.

The Glasshouse Menagerie steams gently in the dark, a great cage of glass and iron with a canopy of palms. Things move between the leaves: a flash of colour, a ripple of scales, a soft and dignified cough.
The Hall's strangest exhibits are all here, and none of them are entirely stuffed.
The Night Garden opens only after dark. Pale flowers unfold in the gloom, lanterns hang from the vines, and a round stone doorway frames the moon.
Rosalind says that she has never painted a garden she loved so much, because she has never been able to see one clearly.
A heavy iron door at the end of the Hall swings open, and a stair descends into the dark. The air is cold and smells of earth, apples, and old iron. Somewhere below, a lamp is already burning.
The Deep Vaults hold what the Society stored, what it saved, and what it could not bring itself to throw away.
The Forgotten Wing lies at the end of a corridor that appears on no plan. The wallpaper is faded to the colour of milk, and every door is slightly too small.
Cornelia stands at the threshold for a long time. Then she opens it herself.

The Founder's Study is a small, warm room that smells of pipe smoke and ink. A fire has been laid in the grate. A chair is drawn up to a desk, and a cup of tea stands on the blotter, with the steam just beginning to fade.
Nobody is there. Everybody holds their breath anyway.

Behind a suit of armour, a stair leads into the walls of the Hall. The Hidden Passage winds on, narrow and low, past little doors and little lamps and the faint sound of a clock that is trying not to be heard.
Barnaby counts the steps. He loses count at three hundred and eleven.

The Chart Room of Lost Lands is a circular room of silent maps. Every wall is covered in charts of places that are not on any other chart: coasts no one has landed on, mountains no one has climbed, seas that were only ever rumoured.
Zephyrine Blackwood takes off her hat, for the first time in the whole of the Hall.

The Grand Ballroom is a hall of mirrors and chandeliers, with a floor of waxed oak that has not known a dancer in twenty years. Dust sheets cover a hundred chairs, and a little gold clock hangs high above the bandstand.
It is the loveliest room in the Hall, and the saddest. It was built for a party that never took place.

The Clock Tower rises over the Hall like a great stone mast. Within it, stair after stair of iron winds up around the great pendulum, and the whole building ticks with the slow heartbeat of a very large and very patient machine.
A single pigeon watches from a beam. It has been watching for a long time.

The last stair ends in the Attic of Marvels, a huge, low, dusty space under the roof, crowded with trunks and crates and things under sheets. Light falls through a round window onto a rocking horse, a lantern, and a well.
It is the oddest room in the Hall, and the one that was kept for last.

A reedy voice drifts down from the east rafters, along with a few feathers. Professor Aldous Finch, ornithologist and absent-minded guardian of the natural history wings, has been living up there with the swifts for twenty years, and has just noticed that someone has opened the doors.
panels.subject: Professor Aldous Finch, a thin absent-minded elderly ornithologist in a rumpled tweed coat with binoculars round his neck, leans out from the east rafters of a great Victorian museum hall among swifts and a few drifting feathers, peering down in surprise through his spectacles; warm evening light through high windows

panels.caption: A man in a very good coat is leaning in the doorway of the Hall of Feathers, as if he owned it. Sam Vane, collector, rival, and charming rogue of the Society, has heard about the restoration. He would like to see what has been done to the place. He would also like to see what is still lying about.
panels.subject: Sam Vane, a suave man in his thirties in a very good dark frock coat, leans in the open doorway of a Victorian bird gallery with a charming half smile, as if he owned the place, glancing at the cases of birds; warm evening light

panels.caption: Among the ferns of the Conservatory, a young man stands very still, holding a watering can. Mark Bloom has been tending the living collections in secret for twenty years, and he is not at all sure he is ready to be seen.
panels.subject: Mark Bloom, a shy young gardener in a canvas apron with soil on his hands, stands very still among tall ferns in an overgrown Victorian conservatory, holding a watering can and looking startled; green evening light

panels.caption: The smell of baking arrives before she does. Anjali Bose, expedition chef and confectioner, sweeps into the Hall with a basket on each arm, takes one look at the Tea Room, and rolls up her sleeves.
From deep within the Hall, a great brass gear begins to turn. Hugo Pemberton, clockwork engineer, has heard the clocks ticking again, and has come, spanner in hand, to see who has been winding them.

A pair of spectacles glints at the top of the Archives stair. Prudence Quill, the Society's exacting archivist, has watched the Hall wake up through a skylight for weeks, and has finally come to tell everyone where they have been filing things wrong.

A woman in a salt-stained coat sits on the Court Bench with a rolled chart across her knees. Zephyrine Blackwood, cartographer, has just come back from the edge of the world, and she has a message that she is not quite ready to deliver.

A sweep of lavender silk, a faint scent of roses, and a very long umbrella. Rosalind Thorne, botanical illustrator and the Society's patroness, has come to see whether the Hall is worth the twenty years of her subscription, and has a secret she was asked to keep.

Volume I: The Hall Wakes. The gates are open, the Atrium is lit, and the first wings have been restored. A rival collector arrives in the Hall of Feathers, and the Society's old rhythm begins, at last, to turn.
The founder's bust looks on from the stairs, and for the first time in twenty years, it seems to approve.
Volume II: The Deep Water. The Shell and Coral Room is restored, and with it comes a confession: Sam Vane was not looking for treasure. He was looking for the founder.
In the glass of the Kraken's Eye, a small square box can be seen, far below, on the floor of the Aquarium.
Volume III: The Box in the Aquarium. The Great Aquarium fills, and a small brass box can be seen at last on the floor of the tank, with a lock on it and a tag. A diver is sent for.
The members of the Society gather around the tea urn for the first time, and begin to feel like a society.

Volume IV: Where I Shall Be. The Great Relief Model rises from its crates, and the Map Room is whole. On the Atlas Lectern, a page lies open to a blank map with a single title, in the founder's own hand.
The Library is next, and the founder's own folio.

Volume V: The Founder's Folio. The Library of Expeditions is restored, and the blue-bound folio is opened at last. The final page reads: The Hall was never meant to be finished. It was meant to be kept.
Several pages have been cut out, with a very sharp blade, and nobody knows by whom.
